name: Vera Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a team lead on days at a medicines distribution warehouse. We send boxes of tablets, dressings and insulin to about four hundred pharmacies and two hospitals. I start at seven, check the overnight orders, and then I'm picking and training at the same time. I'm one of three people trusted with the locked cage for controlled drugs, which I'm quietly proud of.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the best part of it, and what's the hard part?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The best part is that it matters. If we send the wrong strength of a heart tablet, someone could get hurt, so accuracy is everything and I'm good at it. The hard part is the walking, I do about eighteen kilometres a shift, and the scanners freeze when it's busy. My partner Tomasz drives a city bus, so between us we know every early alarm going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first scenario is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was oversold, but I'm glad it helps with the boring bits. I'd probably post a joke about the scanner still freezing despite all the hype. At work I'd say, right, back to normal, let's get the hospital orders out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it means my job is steady. Medicine doesn't stop, because people get sick in every economy. I'd be thinking more about the rent and about whether Tomasz and I can save for a flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do and maybe ask for the next pay band, because I'm training half the new starters anyway. I'd keep using the AI chat now and then to word emails to HR, like I already do. And we'd keep putting about two hundred a month into the flat fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. A bit flat, maybe, because I'd half hoped something would make the walking easier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said accuracy is everything. Does any of the small AI stuff touch that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. If the software spots that someone ordered 100 boxes instead of 10, that's a real help. But the hands in the cage are still mine, and I still count the controlled drugs twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So what's actually on your mind in this world, if not AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Housing, honestly. Our landlord put the rent up eight percent this year. That's more of a worry than any robot.

say: AI was **oversold**, though it helps a little with the **boring bits**.
Medicines still need **sending out**, so it's back to normal at work.
think: My job is **steady** because people need **medicine** in any economy.
The bigger worry is **rent** and saving for a **flat** with Tomasz.
do: **Ask for** the next pay band, since she already trains new starters.
Keep using an **AI chat** now and then to word emails to HR.
Keep saving **£200 a month** into the flat fund.
feel: **Calm**, with a little **disappointment** that the walking stays the same.
S0.quote: Medicine doesn't stop, because people get sick in every economy.
fieldNote: She draws security from the **medicines sector**, not from her own skills alone.
Housing costs, an **eight percent rent rise**, outrank AI as a worry.
She already uses AI **now and then**, so she isn't scared of small tools.

steps.text: Ask the manager for the next pay band for training new starters
Keep putting £200 a month into the flat deposit fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next scenario is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say workers have to share in what this saves, otherwise it's just profit for the owners. I'd probably share some articles about unions negotiating over AI. At work I'd tell my team that the office will feel it before we do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm fine for a few years, but the stuff around me shifts. The ordering and the stock checks will be done by software, and that's part of what makes me senior. If I'm just a fast pair of hands in a medicines warehouse, I'm easier to replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to be on whatever pilot team tests the new stock system, once I've seen it works at the other site. I'd join the union properly instead of just meaning to. I'd keep the flat savings going but maybe hold off on viewing places for a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I think. Not frightened, but alert, like when you hear a noise downstairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does the shrinking show up first in your building?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the office upstairs. Two of the stock controllers checking pharmacy returns, that's exactly the checking and planning the software would do. I know both of them, they come down and have lunch with us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you be worried about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya on my team, who's brilliant but can't read English well, so the new screens would be hard for her. And honestly the stock controllers. I'd worry they'd be moved down to picking and then the picking team would be bigger than it needs to be.

say: Workers must **share the savings**, or it's just **profit** for owners.
The **office** will feel this before the warehouse floor does.
think: I'm **safe for now**, but software takes the **stock checks**.
Without the planning work, I'm just **fast hands**, and easier to replace.
do: **Volunteer** for the new stock-system pilot once it's proven elsewhere.
**Join the union** properly instead of only meaning to.
Keep **flat savings** going but delay house viewings by a year.
feel: **Alert** rather than frightened, like hearing a **noise downstairs**.
S1.quote: If I'm just a fast pair of hands in a medicines warehouse, I'm easier to replace.
fieldNote: She sees her **seniority** resting partly on thinking tasks that software takes.
Her worry for colleagues is specific: **Priya** and the **stock controllers**.
Steady by nature, she waits for **proof elsewhere** before volunteering.

steps.text: Volunteer for the stock-system pilot after it works at the other site
Sign up as a full union member this year
Keep the flat savings going but delay viewings for a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next scenario is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need the government to step in now, with retraining and some kind of income guarantee. I'd be at the rallies, I think, which I've never done. Online I'd say this is the biggest shift in work ever, and it can't just be left to the market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the warehouse job I'm good at won't exist past 2031. My partner drives a bus, which is the other thing everyone says gets automated, so it's not one income at risk, it's both of ours. Tomasz knows it too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd sit down with Tomasz and stop the flat plan. We'd keep renting and put everything into a cushion, maybe three hundred a month. I'd look at nursing assistant training, because I already know medicines and hospitals will still need people at a bedside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, but in a planning way. I'd make lists, that's what I do when I'm scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The thinking AI comes in 2028, the robots in 2031. What does that gap mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The gap means I keep earning while the office goes in 2028, and I watch it happen. That gives me three years to train for something hands-on that robots can't do as well. It's not much, but it's not nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Tomasz talk about at the kitchen table?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd talk about whether to have kids at all in the next few years. We'd said maybe at thirty. In that world, I don't know if we'd risk it with both jobs in danger.

say: The **government** must act now with retraining and an **income guarantee**.
I'd go to **rallies**, because this can't be left to the market.
think: Tomasz drives a bus, so **both our incomes** are at risk.
do: **Stop the flat plan** and keep renting for now.
Put **£300 a month** into a cushion instead of a deposit.
Look into **nursing assistant** training using her medicines knowledge.
S2.quote: My partner drives a bus, which is the other thing everyone says gets automated, so it's not one income at risk, it's both of ours.
fieldNote: The **double risk** to her and her bus-driver partner drives the alarm.
She treats the **three-year gap** as training time for bedside care.
Family plans shift: having **children at thirty** becomes uncertain.

steps.text: Join rallies calling for retraining and an income guarantee
Switch the £300 a month from flat deposit to emergency cushion
Apply for nursing assistant training at the local hospital
Put off the plan to have children at thirty

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next scenario is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same thing about government and retraining, but a bit calmer. Five years is time to get a plan through parliament if people push. I'd be pushing, through the union mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I can do this properly. I'd be thirty-two when the thinking AI lands and thirty-five when the robots come for picking, so I'd have time to train while still being paid. I still think the warehouse job goes, just later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time healthcare course in the first year, two evenings a week, while staying team lead. I'd ask the company to pay for some of it, they do that sometimes. We'd keep saving for the flat but at a smaller amount.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but with five years I'd feel like I had my hands on the wheel, and that's the difference from two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does five years change the kids question?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does, a bit. With five years we might still try for a baby around thirty, but only if one of us has moved into something steadier first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Priya on your team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Priya to start an English course now, while it's still cheap and there's time. Then the new screens and any retraining would be open to her too.

say: Five years is enough to get a **plan through parliament** if people push.
I'd do that pushing mostly through the **union**.
think: I can **train while still paid**, since robots reach picking around 2034.
The warehouse job **still goes**, just later.
do: Start a **part-time healthcare** course two evenings a week.
Ask the company to **pay part** of the course fees.
Keep saving for the flat at a **smaller amount**.
feel: Worried, but with her **hands on the wheel**.
S3.quote: with five years I'd feel like I had my hands on the wheel, and that's the difference from two years.
fieldNote: Five years turns her fear into a **training plan** while still earning.
Having a baby now depends on one of them **moving to steadier work** first.
Her advice to Priya, **learn English now**, shows her team-lead instinct.

steps.text: Start a part-time healthcare course two evenings a week
Ask the union to back company-paid course fees
Keep saving for the flat, at a smaller monthly amount

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next scenario is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair warning, so there's no excuse for anyone to be left behind. I'd be asking our MP what the plan is. At work I'd say let's use the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be about forty when robots can do my job. That's when I'd want to be settled, with kids and a mortgage. So the danger lands right in the middle of the life I'm planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd keep my job, buy the flat if we can, and use AI tools a bit more at work since everyone else would be. Around year three I'd start a healthcare qualification part-time, so it's done by the time the office changes in 2036. And I'd keep voting for parties that talk seriously about retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine day to day, but there's a shadow over the plans. It's like planning a wedding and knowing there'll be a storm sometime that year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be doing in year one versus year five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one is normal life with a bit of extra saving. Year five is when I'd want the qualification half done. I'm not someone who jumps first, but with ten years I don't have to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of this picture you'd welcome?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, yes. If robots take the eighteen kilometres of walking a shift, I won't miss my feet hurting, but I want to still be paid for something.

say: Ten years is **fair warning**, so nobody should be **left behind**.
I'd ask our **MP** what the actual plan is.
think: Robots reach my job around **forty**, right when I want to be **settled**.
The danger lands in the **middle of the life** I'm planning.
do: **Buy the flat** in year one if prices allow.
Start a **healthcare qualification** part-time around year three.
feel: Fine day to day, but with a **shadow** over long-term plans.
S4.quote: If robots take the eighteen kilometres of walking a shift, I won't miss my feet hurting, but I want to still be paid for something.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her **keep the flat plan** and pace her retraining.
She'd **welcome** robots taking the walking, if the **pay** continues.
The threat lands near **forty**, when she expects children and a mortgage.

steps.text: Keep leading the day team and buy the flat if prices allow
Keep working as team lead for the first few years
Start a part-time healthcare qualification around year three
Ask the local MP about retraining plans and vote on it

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it hits me and Tomasz at the same time and we'd have to drop the flat and maybe the kids. What would help is retraining that's actually paid, so I could do a nursing course without losing a wage. And some guarantee that if both of us are out, we don't lose the roof.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the medicines themselves. If robots pick heart pills, someone still needs to be checking. I'd want to be that someone. I'd want to be the person who catches a robot's mistake before a patient does.

headlineQuote: I'd want to be the person who catches a robot's mistake before a patient does.
portrait: Vera, 27, leads the day team at a **medicines warehouse** and holds the controlled-drugs keys.
She values **accuracy** and sees her work as protecting patients.
Her partner Tomasz drives a bus, so fast AGI threatens **both incomes**.
In fast scenarios she drops the flat plan and eyes **nursing assistant** training.
With more time she paces retraining and keeps **family plans** alive.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it hits both her and **Tomasz** at once.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** so she can study nursing without losing a wage.
A **guarantee** that the household keeps its home if both lose work.
